questions.q: According to this lesson, what is a 'quick win' in a multi-year zero trust rollout?
options: A multi-year identity and segmentation project completed in year one
A SaaS security posture management rollout across every application
A near-term change — like enforcing MFA everywhere — that reduces real risk without needing the foundational work to exist first
A maturity scorecard presented to the board
questions.explain: Quick wins land in roughly the first six months and reduce real risk on their own, earning credibility and budget for the foundational work that follows — they aren't the program itself.

questions.q: Why is foundational work described as 'slow and mostly invisible'?
options: Because it's where identity becomes the real control plane and segmentation replaces the flat network — work most people outside security never see directly
Because it only involves marketing material about zero trust
Because it is entirely outsourced to a vendor and never touches internal systems
Because it happens only after long-haul initiatives are complete
questions.explain: Foundational work spans roughly months six through eighteen and builds the identity and segmentation layer everything later depends on, which is exactly why it has to be sequenced early even though it's hard to show off.

questions.q: Why can't micro-segmentation policy decisions work well without identity signals already in place?
options: Because segmentation requires a hardware firewall upgrade first
Because segmentation is only relevant to on-premises networks
Because identity signals are generated by segmentation controls, not the other way around
Because a segment-level access decision on device compliance or 'who is this' has nothing to evaluate if that identity signal doesn't exist yet
questions.explain: Segmentation policy depends on identity signals as its input — without continuous access evaluation and device compliance already feeding it, there's nothing for the segment boundary to base a decision on.

questions.q: What should a real roadmap line name, beyond the initiative's name, according to this lesson?
options: Only the vendor selected to implement it
The horizon it belongs to, what earlier initiative it depends on, and what specifically changes for users and attackers once it ships
The internal project code name only
The number of support tickets it is expected to generate
questions.explain: Specificity like 'standing admin access to production is gone; elevation expires in four hours' is what separates a real roadmap line from a vague initiative name like 'implement conditional access.'

questions.q: What is the correct sequencing relationship this lesson argues for?
options: Long-haul initiatives should be started first to show results quickly
Segmentation should be built before identity work, since segmentation protects the network perimeter
Identity work leads, segmentation follows identity, and data/app/workload-level controls follow segmentation
All three horizons should be executed simultaneously regardless of dependencies
questions.explain: Because each horizon depends on the signals or containment the previous one provides, identity has to lead, segmentation follows identity, and everything else follows segmentation.
